en: The Sūtra on the Merit of the Fundamental Vows of the Seven Buddhas of the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Yijing at Foguang Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavān was traveling through various countries for the purpose of teaching and transforming beings when he arrived at the city of Vaiśālī. He stayed beneath the Tree of Musical Sound (*Ratana-ghoṣa*) together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus and thirty-six thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, among whom were the bodhisattvas Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, Maitreya, and Subhūti.
The Bodhisattvas— Mahāmati Bodhisattva, Vimalamati Bodhisattva, Śailaśikhara Bodhisattva,
Pratibhānaśikhara Bodhisattva, Merudharasikhara Bodhisattva, Amogha-vikrāmin Bodhisattva,
Sūkṣmasvara Bodhisattva, Nityacintin Bodhisattva, and Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva— and other such great [Bodhisattvas].
With bodhisattvas as their leaders, and surrounded by a vast assembly of kings,
ministers, brahmins, householders, the eight classes of devas and nāgas, humans, and non-humans, who all paid respectful homage,
he preached the Dharma— excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, with elegant phrasing and profound meaning, and pure...
First, they are perfectly complete, pure, and brilliant white, bearing the marks of the Brahma-conduct;
they instruct, benefit, and gladden others, causing all to be fully endowed with subtle and wondrous vows and practices, and leading them toward great enlightenment.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Dharmaputra rose from his seat, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority. He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Now there is a vast assembly of immeasurable humans and devas who have all gathered like clouds to hear the Dharma.

We pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will consider all the buddha-fields throughout immeasurable kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, from the time he first resolved his mind for enlightenment until the present; there is nothing therein that you do not know or see.

We pray that, out of compassion, you will expound for us and for the sentient beings of future ages during the Semblance Dharma period the names of the Buddhas, the merits of their original vows, the adornments of their lands, and the various characteristics of their skillful means, so that all who hear them may have their karmic obstructions eliminated and attain non-retrogression until they reach Bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

Mañjuśrī! Out of great compassion, you have taken pity upon sentient beings burdened by immeasurable karmic obstructions, who suffer from various diseases, sorrows, and afflictions; for the sake of their attaining peace and happiness, you have exhorted me to speak of the names of the Buddhas, their original vows and merits, and the adornments of their lands.
"This has been prompted by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, which has caused you to pose this question.
Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well;
I shall explain it for you. Mañjuśrī said:
“Please explain this for us; we long to hear it. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“To the east of here, passing beyond Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of four Gaṅgā rivers, there is a world named Anabhibhūta. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One, named Śubhakīrtiśrīrāja. He is surrounded by an immeasurable assembly of billions of non-regressive Bodhisattvas and currently resides upon a lion throne, magnificently adorned with the seven precious jewels, preaching the Dharma.”

Mañjuśrī! That buddha-field is pure and magnificently adorned, extending for an equal distance of one hundred thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth. Its ground is made of Jambū-river gold, level and soft, with a fragrance like that of the heavens.
It is devoid of the various evil destinies and even the name of "woman," and it contains no shards, pebbles, sand, stones, or thorns.
Rows of jewel trees stand in orderly succession, their flowers and fruits flourishing in abundance;
there are many bathing pools, all adorned with foundations of gold, silver, pearls, and various precious gems.
Mañjuśrī! The bodhisattvas in that land are all born by transformation within lotuses made of the seven treasures.
Therefore, sons and daughters of good family with pure faith should all aspire to be reborn in that Buddha-land.
“Mañjuśrī! That Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, when first generating the mind of enlightenment and practicing the bodhisattva path, made eight great vows.”
What are the eight? "The first great vow:

May it be that when I attain unexcelled Bodhi in a future world, if there are sentient beings whose bodies are oppressed by various sufferings of illness—tormented by fevers, various malarial fevers, sorcery, malevolent spells, or reanimated ghosts; [may they all be relieved]."
If one can invoke my name with a sincere heart, by the power of this, all suffering from illness shall be completely extinguished, even unto the attainment of unsurpassed bodhi.
"The second great vow:
May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are blind, deaf, mute, afflicted with leprosy, or driven mad, and are tormented by various diseases;
if they can invoke my name with a sincere heart, by the power thereof, may their faculties become complete, their various diseases be extinguished, and this continue until they reach Bodhi."
"The third great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who, being entangled and oppressed by greed, hatred, and delusion, commit the sins of immediate retribution and various evil deeds, slander the True Dharma, and fail to cultivate wholesome virtues, such that they are destined to fall into hell and undergo all manner of suffering—if they can sincerely invoke my name, by the power of this act, may their sins of immediate retribution and all karmic obstructions be completely extinguished;
and may there be no sentient beings who fall into the evil realms, but instead constantly enjoy the supreme peace and happiness of humans and devas until they reach Bodhi."
"The fourth great vow:
May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who lack clothing, food, necklaces, bedding, wealth, treasures, incense, flowers, or music;
if they can sincerely invoke my name, by the power of this, may all their deficient necessities of life be fully provided for, until they reach Bodhi."
"The fifth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings whose bodies are bound by shackles and fetters, or who are subjected to whippings and endure various sufferings and afflictions;
if they can sincerely invoke my name, by the power of this act, may they all be liberated from their suffering and reach even unto Bodhi."
"The Sixth Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings in perilous places who are tormented by various evil beasts—bears, *pārśva* bears, lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, vipers, snakes, and scorpions—and whose lives are about to be cut short, such that they cry out in loud wails while undergoing great suffering;

if they can sincerely invoke my name, by the power thereof, may all their terrors be liberated, and may all those evil beasts give rise to hearts of compassion, so that [the beings] always obtain peace and happiness until they reach Bodhi."
“The Seventh Great Vow:
May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who, due to quarreling and litigation, give rise to anxiety and distress;
if they can sincerely invoke my name, by the power thereof, their disputes shall be resolved, and they shall face one another with hearts of loving-kindness until they reach Bodhi.”
"The Eighth Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who enter the rivers or seas and encounter a great violent wind blowing their ships, finding no islands or shores to rely upon and thus giving rise to extreme anxiety and fear;

if they can sincerely invoke my name, by the power thereof, may they all have their wishes fulfilled, reaching places of peace and security, experiencing all manner of happiness until they reach Bodhi."
“Mañjuśrī! These are the eight kinds of subtle and sublime great vows that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, made while practicing the bodhisattva path.”

Furthermore, from the time he first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], that World-Honored One has constantly used the power of meditative concentration to bring sentient beings to maturity, make offerings to all Buddhas, and adorn and purify Buddha-lands, such that his retinue of bodhisattvas is entirely complete.

This merit is inconceivable; even if all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas were to speak for many kalpas, they could not exhaust it, with the sole exception of the Tathāgatas and the bodhisattvas who are in their final birth.

Mañjuśrī! If there are men or women of pure faith—whether kings, ministers, elders, or householders—who, desiring merit and wishing to sever all afflictions, invoke the name of that Buddha, read this sūtra, and with a sincere heart revere, honor, and make offerings to that Tathāgata, then all their evil karmic obstructions and various sufferings of illness shall be entirely extinguished. Whatever they may seek or aspire to shall be fulfilled according to their wishes, and they shall attain non-retrogression until they reach bodhi.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! To the east of here, passing beyond Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of five Gaṅgā Rivers, there is a world named Ratnavatī. There dwells the Buddha named Ratnacandraprajñāvyūhaghoṣeśvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently surrounded by immeasurable billions of bodhisattvas and preaching the Dharma, expounding the subtle, profound, and wondrous meanings of the Mahāyāna."
“Mañjuśrī! That Buddha-Tathāgata, from the time he first resolved his mind upon the bodhisattva path, made eight great vows.
What are these eight?

"First Great Vow: May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings whose minds are disturbed by the pursuit of agriculture or commerce, thereby neglecting the cultivation of Bodhi and sublime wholesome dharmas, remaining unable to escape the cycle of birth and death and each undergoing boundless suffering;

if they can sincerely invoke my name, by the power thereof, may their clothing, food and drink, and necessities of life, as well as gold, silver, and rare treasures, be sufficiently provided according to their wishes; may all their roots of goodness increase, and may they never abandon the Bodhicitta; may they be liberated from the sufferings of all evil realms until they reach Bodhi."
"The Second Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, for all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions who are oppressed by cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and undergo great suffering and affliction—if they can sincerely invoke my name, by the power of this act, their karmic offenses from previous lives shall be entirely extinguished; they shall cast off all suffering and affliction, receive the joys of humans and devas, and continue thus until they reach Bodhi."
"The third great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are women in the worlds of the ten directions whose minds are constantly shrouded by the affliction of lustful desire, who undergo continuous pregnancy—a state deeply loathsome—and who experience great suffering when the time of birth approaches;

if my name should briefly pass through their ears, or if they should recite and remember it, by the power of this, may all their sufferings be eliminated, and after casting off this body, may they always become men until they reach Bodhi."
"The fourth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who, together with their parents, brothers, sisters, wives, children, kinsmen, or various friends and associates, travel through dangerous places and are assailed by bandits, suffering all manner of afflictions;
if they should even briefly hear my name or recite it, by the power of this, may they be liberated from all hardships until they reach Bodhi."
"The fifth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who, while performing various tasks during the darkness of night, are tormented and disturbed by malevolent spirits and ghosts, and thus experience extreme distress and suffering;

may they, upon briefly hearing my name or reciting it, by the power of this act, pass from darkness into light, and may those malevolent spirits and ghosts give rise to thoughts of compassion toward them until they reach Bodhi."

"The sixth great vow: May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who commit base and evil deeds, do not believe in the Triple Gem, possess meager wisdom, and do not cultivate wholesome dharmas— failing to practice the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), the path (*mārga*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and *dhāraṇī*— if they can sincerely invoke my name,

by the power of this act, may their wisdom gradually increase, they shall fully study and practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and they shall have deep faith in the Triple Gem until they reach Bodhi."
"The seventh great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings whose inclinations are base and inferior who dwell in the practice of the paths of the Two Vehicles, having turned their backs on supreme and wondrous Bodhi;
if they can sincerely invoke my name, may they abandon the views of the Two Vehicles and attain non-retrogression from supreme enlightenment until they reach Bodhi."
“Eighth Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who, seeing the kalpa approaching its end and the fires about to break out, give rise to great anxiety and fear, suffering and weeping in grief;

and because of the power of evil karma from their previous lives, undergo these manifold sufferings without any refuge—if they can sincerely invoke my name, may all their anxieties and pains be completely extinguished, and they shall receive the joy of cool serenity. Then, at the end of this life, they shall be born by transformation within a lotus flower in my Buddha-land, constantly cultivating wholesome dharmas until they reach Bodhi.”
“Mañjuśrī! These were the eight kinds of subtle and sublime great vows made by that Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, when he was practicing the bodhisattva path.”
Furthermore, the buddha-field where that Tathāgata dwells is vast, magnificent, and pure, with ground as level as the palm of a hand.

It is lined with celestial trees of exquisite fragrance, covered everywhere by celestial flowers, and celestial music constantly resounds. Celestial bells and chimes are suspended everywhere, and lion thrones are adorned with celestial jewels. The grounds are paved with celestial gems, and there are many wonderful bathing pools;

the earth is soft and supple, free of shards or rubble, and devoid of women and all afflictions. Its inhabitants are exclusively a multitude of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, born through transformation from lotus flowers.
Whenever a thought arises, food, clothing, and all necessary requisites appear before them at will; therefore, it is called the World of Wondrous Jewels. "Mañjuśrī!

If there are men or women of pure faith, kings, princes, ministers, high officials, ladies of the inner court, or court ladies, who during the six periods of day and night, with earnest and sincere hearts, reverently make offerings to that Buddha, the World-Honored One; and who invoke his name, fashion images of him, and present fragrant flowers, music, incense for burning, powdered incense, and unguents; and who remain pure and clean for seven days, observing the eight precepts and giving rise to thoughts of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, vowing to be reborn in that land;

That Buddha-Bhagavān and all the bodhisattvas will protect and keep this person in mind; all their sinful karma will be completely extinguished, and they shall attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi. Greed, hatred, and delusion will gradually become thin and slight; they will be free from all illness and suffering, their lifespan will increase, and whatever they desire shall be fulfilled according to their wishes. All enemies involved in strife will give rise to joy. After casting off this body, they will go to that buddha-field and be born by transformation within a lotus flower. At the moment of birth, their mindfulness, concentration, and dhāraṇīs will all be clearly realized.
Mañjuśrī! You should know that such is the name of that Buddha and his immeasurable merit; if anyone hears it, all their aspirations shall be fulfilled. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

To the east of here, passing through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of six Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Paripūrṇagandhakūṭa. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Suvarṇavarṇaratnarcisucaryāsaṃpanna, who is currently teaching the Dharma, surrounded by immeasurable billions of bodhisattvas.
“Mañjuśrī! That Buddha-Tathāgata, from the time he first resolved his mind upon the bodhisattva path, made four great vows. What are these four?

“First Great Vow: May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who commit various acts of slaughter and harm, taking the lives of others, and by virtue of these evil karmas undergo the sufferings of the hells;

or if, even having attained human form, they are short-lived and plagued by many illnesses, or encounter injury from water, fire, blades, or poison, and must endure the agony of death—if such beings hear my name and call upon me with a sincere heart, by the power of this, may all their evil karmas be completely extinguished, and may they be free from illness, enjoy long life, and not meet with untimely death, until they reach Bodhi.”
"The Second Great Vow:
May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who commit various evil deeds by stealing the wealth of others, and as a result are destined for the evil realms;

or even if they should obtain human birth, they are born into impoverished families, lacking food and clothing, and constantly suffering all manner of pain—if they hear my name and recite it with a sincere heart, by the power of this, may all their evil karma be completely extinguished, and they shall never lack clothing or food until they reach Bodhi."
"The third great vow: May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who treat one another with mutual contempt and harbor enmity toward each other,

should they hear my name and call upon it with a sincere heart, by the power of this act, may they each give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward one another, as toward their own parents, until they reach Bodhi."
"The fourth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings—whether monastics or laypeople, men or women, belonging to the seven assemblies—who are entangled by greed, hatred, and delusion; who violate the precepts established by the Tathāgata and commit various evil deeds, destined to fall into hell and undergo various bitter retributions;

if they hear my name and call upon me with a sincere heart, by the power of this, may all their evil karma be completely extinguished, may they sever all afflictions, reverently uphold the *śīla*, and become well-able to guard their body, speech, and mind, never regressing until they reach Bodhi."
“Mañjuśrī! These are the four kinds of sublime great vows that were made by that Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, when he was practicing the bodhisattva path.”
Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, the buddha-field where that Tathāgata dwells is vast, majestic, and pure; its ground is as level as the palm of a hand and is composed entirely of jewels.
It is constantly fragrant like exquisite sandalwood, and rows of incense trees stand in formation. Divine, exquisite pearl necklaces, maṇi gems, and other precious jewels hang down everywhere.
There are many bathing ponds, adorned with celestial jewels, filled with fragrant waters, and endowed with every excellence; along their four sides hang exquisite silken banners.
The eightfold streets and avenues are magnificently decorated at every turn.
All sentient beings there are free from all afflictions, sorrows, griefs, and sufferings; there are no women, for the majority are bodhisattvas dwelling on the various stages.

Exquisite and wondrous music resounded spontaneously without being struck, expounding the subtle, profound, and sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna; if any sentient beings heard this sound, they would attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed Bodhi.

“Mañjuśrī! By the power of his former vows and through skillful means, that Buddha-Tathāgata accomplished a buddha-field, perfectly adorned and fully embellished. Seated upon the bodhi-seat, he formed this thought:

‘In future ages, if there are sentient beings who are entangled by greed, hatred, and delusion; oppressed by various illnesses; given an opportunity by enemies; or who die an untimely death; and who, further due to their evil karma, fall into the hells and undergo great, intense suffering.’”

That Buddha, seeing these sentient beings afflicted by suffering, spoke this divine mantra to eliminate their karmic obstructions, so that they might receive and uphold it, thereby attaining great benefit in the present life, remaining far removed from all sufferings, and abiding in bodhi.
He then spoke the mantra, saying: "Tadyathā | sīḍi sīḍi susīḍi" |
Moha-cchinna-mukṣaṇi mudite vimudite amale vimale.
Maṅkule he rañje kevi haratna kevi sarvāntasattvānām.
Paramārthasatyanirmadane mahānirmadane.
Ambude amśubude vidhāve subhane.
Varama gokṣaka varama cūḍite
Sarvākārajñatāpratisaṃvid-sarvadharmābhisambodhi-gati.
Jietu shasi naibotuo juti poxiadi (Ccheta-śrī-nirvṛta-koti-prakāśite)
"Namo sarvathāgatānāṃ svāhā. At that time,

when the World-Honored One spoke this mantra of great power and great brilliance, all the great Bodhisattvas in the assembly, as well as the Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra, Brahmā, and others, praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent! O World-Honored One of Great Compassion!”

He is able to proclaim such a great and powerful divine mantra of the Tathāgatas of the past, desiring to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, to exhaust the ocean of afflictions, to ascend the shore of Nirvāṇa, to eliminate diseases, and to fulfill all their aspirations.

The Buddha addressed the great assembly: “If there are men or women of pure faith, kings, princes, ministers, high officials, ladies of the inner court, or court ladies, who desire merit and virtue, and who give rise to a heart of reverent faith toward this divine mantra; if they read it, recite it, or explain its meaning to others; if they give rise to a heart of great compassion for all sentient beings; if they offer sincere worship with incense, flowers, lamps, and candles during the six periods of day and night; if they bathe in purity and observe the eightfold precepts; and if they recite it with utmost sincerity—all their most heavy and boundless karmic obstructions shall be entirely extinguished. In this very life, they shall be free from all afflictions. When their lives are about to end, they will be protected by the Buddhas and will be born through transformation within a lotus flower in that land.”

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! To the east of here, passing beyond Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of seven Gaṅgā rivers, there is a world named Aśoka. There dwells a Buddha named Aśokottamaśrī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides there, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly."

Furthermore, the buddha-field where that Tathāgata dwells is vast, magnificent, and pure; its ground is as level as the palm of a hand, composed entirely of jewels, fine, smooth, and soft, and it is constantly fragrant.
There is no sound of sorrow or suffering, it is free from all afflictions, and there is neither the name of any evil realm nor of women.
Everywhere there are bathing pools with golden embankments, filled to the brim with scented water.
Rows of jewel trees were lined up, their flowers and fruits flourishing and lush;
exquisite music played spontaneously without being struck, just like the majestic adornments of the Land of Immeasurable Life in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
“Mañjuśrī! When that Blessed One was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made four great vows. What are the four?
"First Great Vow: May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future world, if there are sentient beings who are constantly tormented and oppressed by sorrow and suffering;

if they hear my name and invoke it with a sincere heart, by the power of this, may all their grief, lamentation, and various afflictions be entirely extinguished, and may they enjoy long life, peace, and security until they reach Bodhi."
"The Second Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who have committed various evil deeds and are born in the dark places of the Avīci Hell, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction;

because they heard my name in a previous life, at that time I shall emit light from my body to illumine those who suffer. By the power of this, when they see the light, all their karmic obstructions shall be completely extinguished. They shall be liberated from all sufferings, be reborn among humans and devas, and enjoy happiness as they wish until they reach Bodhi."
"The Third Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who commit various evil deeds—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—and consequently suffer the pain of swords and staves in their present existence, destined for rebirth in the evil realms; or even if they obtain a human body, they are short-lived and plagued by many illnesses, born into poor and lowly families where clothing and food are entirely lacking, constantly enduring the sufferings of cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, their bodies devoid of luster, and the relatives they attract being neither virtuous nor kind—if such beings hear my name and call upon me with a sincere heart, by the power of this, may their every wish for food, drink, and clothing be fully satisfied;
may their bodily radiance become as lovely as that of the devas, and may they obtain virtuous kinsmen, until they reach Bodhi."
"The fourth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are constantly harassed and disturbed by yakṣas and various malevolent spirits, having their vital essence stolen and undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction;

if they hear my name and call upon it with a sincere heart, by the power thereof, may all the yakṣas and others be completely dispersed, each giving rise to a mind of compassion, and be liberated from all sufferings until they reach Bodhi."
“Mañjuśrī! These are the four kinds of sublime great vows made by that Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing the name of that Buddha, recite it and pay homage day and night during the six periods, making offerings with a sincere heart and giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, their karmic obstructions will be extinguished; they will be liberated from sorrow and suffering, attain long life free from illness, acquire the knowledge of past lives, be born through transformation within lotus flowers in various Buddha-lands, and be constantly protected by the devas.”

Mañjuśrī! By reciting the name of that Buddha, one can generate such immeasurable meritorious karma; yet the adornments of that buddha-field through the power of his vows and its sublime qualities cannot be known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, except by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! To the east of here, passing beyond Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of eight Gaṅgā rivers, there is a world named Dharmadhvaja. There, a Buddha named Dharmasāgaragarjitasvara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently dwells and expounds the Dharma."

Mañjuśrī! The land where that Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwells is pure and free from defilement; its ground is level and even, composed of crystal, constantly radiant, and filled with fragrant scents.

Its city walls are made of indranīla gems, and it has eight main thoroughfares paved with gold and silver. Its pavilions, halls, soaring eaves, windows, and railings are all adorned and fashioned from various jewels.

Celestial fragrant jewel trees stand in rows everywhere; upon their branches hang celestial silks, and precious bells dangle at every point. When stirred by a gentle breeze, they produce wondrous sounds that proclaim impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. Sentient beings who hear them cast off the entanglements of desire, gradually eliminate their habitual tendencies, and realize profound meditative concentration.
Wondrous celestial incense and flowers fall in profusion.
On its four sides are eight bathing pools, their bottoms strewn with golden sand and filled with fragrant water.
Mañjuśrī! In that buddha-field there are no evil realms of existence, nor are there any women; beings are born through transformation from lotuses, free from all afflictions.
When that Buddha-Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made four great vows.
What are the four? "The first great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings born into families of wrong views who do not produce pure faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and who remain far removed from the mind of unsurpassed Bodhi; [may they all, through my power, abandon such views and give rise to pure faith]."

If they hear my name and call upon it with a sincere heart, by the power of this, their ignorance and false wisdom shall be extinguished day and night; they shall develop deep, correct faith in the Triple Gem and never again regress until they reach Bodhi.
"The Second Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings born in the borderlands who, due to associating with evil friends, commit various sinful deeds and fail to cultivate wholesome qualities, such that the names of the Triple Gem never reach their ears and they fall into the three evil realms after death;
may all such beings, upon briefly hearing my name, have their karmic obstructions eliminated by this power, meet virtuous spiritual friends, and not fall into the evil realms until they reach Bodhi."
"The third great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who lack clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all necessities of life, and because of these conditions give rise to great sorrow and suffering, committing various evil deeds in their pursuit of them;
if they hear my name and call upon it with a sincere heart, by the power of this, whatever they lack shall be obtained according to their thoughts, until they reach Bodhi."
"The fourth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who, due to their past evil karma, engage in mutual strife and contention, inflicting harm upon one another with bows, arrows, swords, and staves;

if they hear my name and call upon it with a sincere heart, by the power of this, may each give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and cease harming one another. If even unwholesome thoughts do not arise within them, how much less would they wish to take the lives of others?"
He constantly practiced joy and equanimity, even unto enlightenment. "Mañjuśrī!
These are the four kinds of subtle and wondrous great vows made by that Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, when he was practicing the bodhisattva path."

If there are men or women of pure faith who, upon hearing the name of that Buddha, pay homage with a sincere heart, make diligent offerings, and uphold, recite, and contemplate [the name], their karmic obstructions will be extinguished; they shall attain the non-retrogressive bodhicitta, possess the wisdom of recollecting past lives, and always behold the Buddhas in every place where they are born. Free from illness and endowed with long life, after the end of their lives, they shall be reborn in that land, where clothing, food, drink, and all necessities of life arrive according to their thoughts, lacking nothing at all.
Mañjuśrī! That Buddha, the World-Honored One, is fully endowed with such immeasurable merits; therefore, sentient beings should always keep him in mind and never allow themselves to forget him.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! To the east of here, passing through Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of nine Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sthitibhadra-ratnasāgara. There, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Dharmasāgaravijayamati-vikrīḍita-abhijña currently dwells and teaches the Dharma."
“Mañjuśrī! When that Buddha-Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made four great vows. What are these four?

"First Great Vow: May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who commit various evil deeds— such as farming and plowing while harming living beings, or engaging in trade while deceiving others, or constantly committing slaughter in the midst of war and conflict—

if they hear my name and call upon it with a sincere heart, by the power of this, may their necessities of life be fulfilled according to their wishes without needing to seek them out, and may they constantly cultivate all manner of goodness until they reach Bodhi."
“The second great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who commit the ten unwholesome deeds, such as the sin of killing, and by reason of these causes and conditions, are destined to fall into hell;
if they hear my name and call upon it with a sincere heart, may they fully accomplish the ten paths of wholesome action, not fall into the evil realms, and continue thus until they reach Bodhi.”
"The third great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who lack self-mastery and are subject to others, or who are imprisoned, bound by shackles, fetters, and stocks, or subjected to the pain of whips and staves, even unto the ultimate punishment;
if they hear my name and call upon it with a sincere heart, by the power of this, may they all be liberated from their calamities and afflictions, even unto the attainment of Bodhi."
"The Fourth Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who commit various evil deeds, do not believe in the Triple Gem, follow false views, reject and turn their backs on correct principles, and take pleasure in heretical associates; if they slander and destroy the Buddha’s sutras, claiming they are not the words of the Sage, and instead respectfully accept and uphold the scriptures of external paths—whether doing so themselves or teaching others to do so—and if they are thus born together in delusion, destined to fall into hell with no prospect of escape; or even if they should obtain human form, they are born in one of the eight difficult states, far removed from the Right Path, blind and lacking the eye of wisdom; [may all such beings be led by me to liberation]."

If such a person hears my name and calls it to mind with a sincere heart, by the power of this, at the time of their death, right mindfulness will manifest before them; they will be liberated from all hardships, always be born in a central land, and enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss until they reach enlightenment.
“Mañjuśrī! These are the four kinds of sublime great vows that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, made while practicing the bodhisattva path.”
Mañjuśrī! That buddha-field, adorned with meritorious qualities, is equal to and no different from the world-system of the Tathāgata Suvicitra-ratna. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

To the east, passing from here through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Vaidūryanirmala; the Buddha there is named Bhaisajyaguruvaidūryaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
“Mañjuśrī! When that Buddha, the World-Honored One, first resolved his mind to practice the bodhisattva path, he made twelve great vows.
What are these twelve?

"First Great Vow: May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, my own radiance shall illuminate boundless realms; with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor signs adorning my body, may all sentient beings become no different from me."
"The second great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, my body shall be like lapis lazuli, pure and transparent both within and without; its radiance vast and expansive, filling all directions and adorned with a network of flames, surpassing the sun and moon. In the dark and obscure places between the Iron Ring Mountains, may beings be able to see one another; or when they travel through the night in this world, may these sentient beings, upon seeing my radiance, all receive illumination and carry out their various tasks accordingly."
"The third great vow:
May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, through immeasurable and boundless wisdom and skillful means, I shall cause all things enjoyed by sentient beings to become inexhaustible."
"The fourth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who walk upon deviant paths, I shall cause them all to travel upon the correct path of Bodhi; and if there are those who practice the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, I shall likewise cause them to dwell securely within the Mahāyāna Dharma."
"The fifth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who practice the pure conduct within my Dharma, may I cause them all to obtain unimpaired precepts, skillfully guarding the three karmas, so that none shall commit transgressions or fall into the evil realms."
Should there be any transgressions committed, upon hearing my name, if they single-mindedly recite and uphold it, confess with a sincere heart, they shall regain purity until they reach Bodhi.
"The sixth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who lack their sense faculties, who are ugly, dull-witted, or paralyzed; who are deaf, blind, mute, or stammering; who are hunchbacked, crippled, or afflicted with leprosy, insanity, or various other sufferings of disease—if such beings hear my name and call upon it with a sincere heart, may they all become upright and dignified, and may all their illnesses be cured."
"The seventh great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are impoverished and suffering, having no place of refuge, oppressed by various illnesses, lacking medicine and physicians;

may all their ailments be dispelled upon briefly hearing my name, their kinsmen increase and flourish, they lack nothing in wealth and resources, and their bodies and minds are peaceful and happy, until they reach Bodhi."

“Eighth Great Vow: May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are women who are oppressed by the manifold sufferings of womanhood and, feeling profound revulsion, wish to cast off their female bodies;
if they hear my name and invoke it with a sincere heart, they shall, in this very life, transform into men, endowed with the marks of a man, until they reach Bodhi.”
"The ninth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, I shall cause all sentient beings to escape the snares of Māra; furthermore, regarding those of various heterodox views, I shall embrace them all, causing them to give rise to right view and gradually lead them to practice the deeds of all Bodhisattvas, up until the attainment of Bodhi."

"The tenth great vow: May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are constrained by royal law, imprisoned in dungeons, bound with shackles and whips, or even subjected to the ultimate punishment, and further beset by numerous bitter sufferings and urgent anxieties such that they find no moment of joy—
if they hear my name, by the power of my merit and majestic spiritual authority, may they all be liberated from all sorrow and suffering, until they reach Bodhi."
"The eleventh great vow:
May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who, tormented by the fire of hunger, commit various evil deeds for the sake of seeking food;

if they hear my name and call upon it with a sincere heart, I shall first satisfy them to their hearts' content with the most excellent and sublime food and drink, and subsequently cause them to abide in supreme bliss through the flavor of the Dharma, until they reach Bodhi."
"The twelfth great vow: May it be that when I attain bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who lack clothing and are tormented by mosquitoes, gadflies, cold, and heat;

if they hear my name and call upon it with a sincere heart, may they immediately obtain all kinds of exquisite garments, precious ornaments, music, incense, and flowers according to their preferences, thereby fulfilling all their needs, being freed from all suffering and affliction, until they reach bodhi."
“Mañjuśrī! These are the twelve sublime and supreme vows that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha made while practicing the bodhisattva path.”
The Sūtra on the Merit of the Fundamental Vows of the Seven Buddhas of Lapis Lazuli Light, Volume One;
The Sūtra on the Merit of the Fundamental Vows of the Seven Buddhas of Lapis Lazuli Light, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang at Foguang Monastery.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:

"The great vows made by that Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha when he was practicing the bodhisattva path, as well as the meritorious adornments of his buddha-field, could not be fully described by me even in an eon, or more than an eon."

Yet that buddha-field is purely and entirely pure, devoid of all defilements of desire; it is likewise free from women, the three evil realms, and even the sound of suffering and affliction. Its ground is made of pure lapis lazuli, and its city walls, gates, palaces, as well as its corridors, halls, eaves, windows, and jeweled nets, are all composed of the seven treasures—just like the meritorious adornments of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

In that land, there were two bodhisattvas: the first named Sunlight Pervading Illumination and the second named Moonlight Pervading Illumination. They served as the leaders among the immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas and were able to uphold the precious treasury of that Buddha’s true Dharma.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī! If there are men or women of pure faith, they should aspire to be born in that Buddha-world. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there are sentient beings who do not recognize good and evil, but harbor only greed and stinginess; who do not know how to practice giving or the karmic rewards of giving; who are foolish and lacking in wisdom, devoid of faith;
who amass precious wealth and labor diligently to guard it; who feel displeasure in their hearts upon seeing a beggar approach;
and who, even when compelled to practice giving, feel as deep a sense of regret as if they were cutting flesh from their own bodies.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable sentient beings who are stingy and greedy; they accumulate wealth and resources, yet they cannot even use them for themselves, let alone provide for their parents, wives, children, slaves, servants, or those who come to beg.
Those sentient beings, when their lives end here, will be reborn among the hungry ghosts or in the realm of animals.

Because they previously heard the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha while in the human world, even though they are in the evil realms, they will still remember the name of that Tathāgata. They will then pass away from those states and be reborn among humans, attaining the knowledge of past lives. Remembering the suffering of the evil realms, they will take no pleasure in sensual desires; they will delight in practicing generosity and praise those who give. Regarding all their wealth and possessions, they will have no heart of stinginess, and gradually they will be able to give their heads, eyes, hands, feet, blood, flesh, and limbs to those who come seeking them—how much more so other material goods?
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! Suppose there is another person who takes refuge in the World-Honored One and receives the various precepts, yet violates the rules of conduct and destroys right view;
or those who uphold the precepts and maintain right view but do not seek extensive learning, and thus cannot comprehend the profound meaning of the sūtras spoken by the Buddha."

Though they may possess great learning, they harbor arrogance; because of this prideful mind, they deem themselves right and others wrong, disparaging and slandering the True Dharma, thereby becoming accomplices of Māra.
Such foolish people, practicing wrong views themselves, further cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sentient beings to fall into great perilous pits.

These sentient beings, having fallen into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, if they have previously heard the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, by the power of that Tathāgata’s original vows, will remember the Buddha’s name while in the hells; when their lives there end, they will return to birth among humans.

Possessing right view and diligence, with a mind that is disciplined and well-tamed, they renounce worldly life to go forth into homelessness. Within the Buddha’s Dharma, they receive and uphold the precepts without violation; endowed with right view and extensive learning, they understand the most profound meanings. Free from arrogance, they do not slander the true Dharma and do not become companions of Māra. They gradually practice all the bodhisattva deeds until reaching enlightenment.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! If there are sentient beings who, being stingy, greedy, and jealous, commit various evil deeds, praising themselves and disparaging others, they shall, at the end of their lives, fall into the three evil realms and undergo intense suffering for immeasurable thousands of years.

When their time there has ended and they are reborn among humans, they may become cattle, horses, camels, donkeys, or similar creatures; they will be constantly subjected to whipping and lashes, their minds tormented by hunger and thirst, their bodies perpetually burdened with heavy loads, and they will be exhausted by misery and toil."
If they obtain human birth, they will be born into lowly and base circumstances as slaves, servants, or laborers, driven by others and never possessing independence.

By the power of the roots of goodness from having heard the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha during their previous lives as humans, they now recall it again and take refuge with a sincere heart. Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, they are liberated from all sufferings; their faculties become sharp and keen, and they possess great wisdom and extensive learning. They constantly seek the supreme Dharma, always encounter virtuous friends, forever sever the snares of Māra, break the shell of ignorance, dry up the river of afflictions, and attain liberation from all birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress, even unto Bodhi.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! If there are sentient beings who delight in estrangement, who engage in mutual strife and litigation, and who disturb themselves and others; who, through body, speech, and mind, create various evil karmas, constantly performing harmful deeds against one another and plotting each other's ruin;

who summon deities of mountains, forests, trees, and burial mounds; who kill living beings and take their flesh and blood to offer as sacrifices to yakṣas, rākṣasas, and other spirits; who write down the names of their enemies or fashion their images, cursing them with malevolent incantations; or who employ sorcery, voodoo, and the raising of corpses to cut off their lives and destroy their bodies."

If these sentient beings hear the name of this Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, none of those evil conditions will be able to harm them. All will develop mutual compassion, seeking their benefit and peace, free from any intent to injure or afflict, as well as any heart of resentment; they will always feel contentment with what they possess.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! If there are members of the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as other men and women of pure faith—who are able to observe the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) for one year, or for three months, and who, having undertaken these precepts, dedicate this root of goodness toward rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) to behold the Buddha Amitāyus."

If one hears the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, at the time of death, eight bodhisattvas will come by means of their supernormal powers to show them the way to their destination; they will then be spontaneously reborn within various multicolored flowers made of many kinds of jewels in that realm.
Some may, because of this, be born in the heavens; though born among the gods, their former roots of goodness are not exhausted, and they shall no longer be reborn in any other evil realms.

When their lifespan in the heavens comes to an end, they return to be born among humans. They may become universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) who rule over the four continents, possessing sovereign majesty and power; they exhort and transform immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, leading them to practice the ten paths of wholesome action.

Alternatively, they may be born into the *kṣatriya*, *brāhmaṇa*, householder, or noble clans, possessing abundant wealth and treasures with granaries overflowing; they are handsome and dignified in appearance, with flourishing retinues, and endowed with intelligence, wisdom, courage, vigor, and great physical strength.
If it is a woman who hears the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha and upholds it with a sincere heart, she shall never again receive a female body hereafter.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! When that Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha attained awakening, by the power of his original vows, he beheld all sentient beings who encounter various sufferings of illness—such as emaciation, malaria, consumption, jaundice, and other diseases—or those afflicted by malevolent spells or sorcery, or those with short lifespans, or those who die untimely deaths; he desired to cause such sufferings of illness to be eliminated and their prayers for fulfillment to be realized."

At that time, the World-Honored One entered a samādhi called "Eliminating the Suffering and Affliction of All Sentient Beings. Having entered this concentration, a great radiance issued forth from his uṣṇīṣa, and within that light he proclaimed this Great Dhāraṇī Mantra:

*Namo bhagavate vīśalyakaro vaiḍūryaprabhā rājāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya | Tadyathā | Oṃ vīśale vīśale vīśalyasamudgate svāhā.* When this mantra had been spoken within the light, the earth shook violently and a great radiance was emitted. The sickness and suffering of all sentient beings were entirely eliminated, and they experienced peaceful and secure bliss.

Mañjuśrī! If you see a man or a woman suffering from illness, you should with single-minded devotion perform purification and rinsing for that patient; then, whether it be food, medicine, or water free of insects, recite over it one hundred and eight times with dhāraṇīs and give it to them to consume, whereby all their illnesses and sufferings will be completely extinguished.

If one has any aspirations, by reciting this with a sincere heart, all shall be fulfilled according to one's wishes; one shall be free from illness and enjoy longevity, and after the end of life, shall be reborn in that world, attaining non-retrogression and proceeding even unto Bodhi.

Therefore, Mañjuśrī! If there be any man or woman who, with a sincere and earnest heart, reverently makes offerings to that Bhagavān Bhaisajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha Tathāgata, they should constantly maintain this mantra and not allow it to be forgotten.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! If there are men or women of pure faith who hear the names of the aforementioned seven Buddhas—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—and having heard them, recite and uphold them; if, at dawn, after chewing tooth-sticks and rinsing their mouths for purification, they make offerings to the images with various flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, and unguents, and perform various musical performances;
and if they either write this sūtra themselves or instruct others to write it, upholding it with single-minded devotion and listening to its meaning;"
One should cultivate offerings toward that Dharma teacher, bestowing all available requisites for sustaining the body so that they lack nothing.
In this way, one will receive the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas, and all aspirations will be fulfilled until the attainment of Bodhi.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

During the period of the Final Dharma, I vow to employ various skillful means to cause all men and women of pure faith to hear the names of the Tathāgatas of the seven Buddhas, even awakening them to these Buddha-names within their dreams.”

"Bhagavān! If one receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, or further explains and reveals it for others; whether writing it oneself or instructing others to write it; honoring and respecting it by making offerings of various kinds of flowers, incense, ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, necklaces, banners, canopies, and music; wrapping it in five-colored silks and brocades; and placing it upon a high seat in a clean, swept location."

At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues and countless hundreds of thousands of other celestial beings, all went to that place to make offerings and provide protection.
“World-Honored One!

Wherever this jewel of a sutra circulates, and for those who receive and uphold it, by virtue of the merit of the original vows of those seven Tathāgatas and the power of the majesty of their names, you should know that in such places there will be no more untimely deaths; nor shall they have their vital essence stolen by malevolent spirits or ghosts. Even if it has already been stolen, it shall be restored to its former state, and body and mind shall be peaceful and happy.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is as you have said, Mañjuśrī!

If there are men or women of pure faith who wish to make offerings to those seven Tathāgatas, they should first respectfully fashion images of the seven Buddhas and place them upon a clean, sublime, and excellent seat; they should scatter flowers, burn incense, and adorn that place with various banners and streamers."
For seven days and seven nights, one should observe the eightfold precepts, eat pure food, bathe the body, and wear new, clean clothes;

with a mind free from defilement and turbidity, and devoid of malice or harm, one should constantly give rise toward all sentient beings to a mind of benefit and happiness, compassion, joy, equanimity, and impartiality;
while playing drums and music and singing songs of praise for their merits, one should circumambulate the Buddha image to the right.
Recalling all the original vows of that Tathāgata, one should read and recite this sutra, contemplate its meaning, and expound and reveal it.

According to their respective wishes, they shall obtain longevity if they seek longevity, wealth if they seek wealth, official rank if they seek rank, and sons or daughters if they seek children; everything shall be fulfilled.

Furthermore, if there should be a person who suddenly has a bad dream, sees various evil omens, or witnesses strange birds gathering, or if hundreds of portents appear within their home—if this person were to reverently make offerings to those Buddhas with the most excellent requisites, then all such bad dreams, evil omens, and inauspicious signs will entirely vanish and be unable to cause any harm.

Should there be fears such as those of water, fire, knives, poison, precipices, treacherous paths, or malevolent elephants, lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, snakes, scorpions, centipedes, and the like—if one can wholeheartedly recollect that Buddha and pay him reverent homage, one shall be liberated from all such terrors.

If a foreign land invades and harasses you, or if thieves and rebels rise up in revolt, those who mindfully and reverently recollect that Tathāgata will find all their enemies completely dispersed and scattered. "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there are men or women of pure faith who, for as long as they live, do not serve other deities, but instead single-mindedly take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts—whether the five precepts, the ten precepts, the twenty-four bodhisattva precepts, the two hundred and fifty bhikṣu precepts, or the five hundred bhikṣuṇī precepts—and should they happen to violate any of these precepts and fear falling into the evil realms, if they can single-mindedly recite the name of that Buddha and reverently make offerings to him, they will certainly not be reborn within the three evil destinies.

If there are women who, when the time of childbirth approaches, undergo extreme suffering, should they be able to single-mindedly invoke the names, pay homage, praise, revere, and make offerings to the seven Tathāgatas, all their sufferings will be eliminated. The child they give birth to will have a handsome and upright countenance, bringing joy to all who see him; he will possess sharp faculties and intelligence, be free from illness and live in peace and happiness, and no non-human beings shall steal away his vital essence.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
“The praise I have offered regarding the merit of the names of those seven Tathāgatas constitutes the profound realm of all Buddhas, which is difficult to comprehend; do not give rise to doubt.”
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the profound meaning of the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, I harbor no doubt or confusion.”
Why is this so? Because, World-Honored One, all the physical, verbal, and mental actions of all Tathāgatas are entirely free from falsehood.
World-Honored One!
These orbs of the sun and moon might be made to fall;
Sumeru, the king of mountains, might be caused to tremble;
but that which is spoken by the Buddhas can never be otherwise.
“World-Honored One!
Yet there are sentient beings who lack the faculty of faith; upon hearing the discourse on the profound realm of the Buddhas, they will think:
‘How can one obtain such merit and benefits merely by recollecting the names of the seven Buddhas?’”
"Because of this lack of faith, they will give rise to slander.
Throughout the long night, they will lose great benefit and happiness, falling into the various evil destinies.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If those sentient beings should hear the names of the Buddhas with their ears, it is impossible for them to fall into the evil realms, except in the case of fixed karma that cannot be altered."
Ānanda! This is the profound realm of all Buddhas, difficult to believe and understand.
That you are able to believe and accept it should be known as entirely due to the majestic power of the Tathāgata.
Ānanda! All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to know this, with the sole exception of bodhisattvas who are in their last birth before buddhahood. Ānanda!
A human body is difficult to obtain;
to have faith, reverence, and respect for the Triple Gem is likewise difficult to obtain;
and to hear the names of the Tathāgatas of the seven Buddhas is even more difficult than that.

Ānanda! Those Tathāgatas possess immeasurable bodhisattva practices, immeasurable skillful means, and immeasurable vast vows. Such practices, vows, and skillful means—I could not finish describing them even in one kalpa, or more than one kalpa.

At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Jue-tuo (Trāṇamukta). He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the future final age, when the Semblance Dharma arises, if there are sentient beings who are oppressed and tormented by various illnesses and sufferings, their bodies becoming emaciated and weak, unable to eat or drink, their throats and lips parched, their vision darkening until they see only shadows, and the signs of death appearing before them, while their parents, relatives, friends, and acquaintances weep as they surround them.
While lying upon their original beds, they see the messengers of Yama, the King of Dharma, who lead their *vijñāna* (consciousness) away to the presence of the King.

Now, every sentient being has an innate deity (*sahaja-deva*) who records all the virtuous and non-virtuous deeds they have committed and presents them to that King. The King then interrogates them according to the law regarding their actions and passes judgment in accordance with their merits and faults.
At that time, if the patient’s relatives and friends can take refuge in the Buddhas on their behalf, adorning them with various ornaments and making offerings according to the Dharma.

Then that consciousness, after passing seven days, or two weeks, or even up to seven weeks, awakens as if from a dream and regains its original spirit. It then personally recalls and knows the retributive fruits obtained from wholesome and unwholesome karmas. Because it has personally witnessed that the retribution of karma is not in vain, it will not commit evil even at the cost of its life.
Therefore, men and women of pure faith should all receive and uphold the names of these seven Buddhas, and according to their respective capacities, pay them respectful offerings.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta:
"Good son, what is the method for reverently making offerings to those seven Tathāgatas?"
The Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta said: "Virtuous One!
If there is a sick person or anyone else beset by calamities whom one wishes to deliver, one should observe the eightfold precepts for seven days and seven nights on their behalf."
One should provide food, drink, and other requisites for the Buddha and the Sangha according to what one possesses;
during the six periods of day and night, one should reverently prostrate to the seven Tathāgatas and recite this sutra forty-nine times;

one should light forty-nine lamps and fashion seven images of those Tathāgatas, placing seven lamps before each image, with the lamps being circular in shape like chariot wheels, such that their light remains unceasing until the forty-ninth night.
One should fashion forty-nine banners of various colors, along with one long banner forty-nine feet in length;
furthermore, one should release forty-nine living beings.
By doing so, one will be able to escape calamities and hardships, and shall not be seized by various accidents or malevolent spirits.
"Venerable Ānanda!
This is the ritual for making offerings to the Tathāgatas.

If anyone, among these seven Buddhas, makes an offering by invoking the name of even one Buddha, they shall all obtain such immeasurable merit and have their aspirations fulfilled; how much more so if they are able to make offerings complete unto all of them?"
"Furthermore, Venerable Ānanda! If calamities should arise for a Kṣatriya consecrated king, such as: the calamity of pestilence among the populace; the calamity of invasion by foreign nations;

the calamity of rebellion within one's own realm; the calamity of portents in the stars and constellations; the calamity of eclipses of the sun and moon; the calamity of unseasonable wind and rain; or the calamity of drought when the time for rain has passed—at that time, that Kṣatriya consecrated king should give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, issue a great general amnesty, and deliver those beings who are in dark dungeons, distress, and suffering. Then, according to the aforementioned ritual, he should make offerings to the Buddhas."

By virtue of these roots of goodness and the power of that Tathāgata’s original vow, his realm shall immediately attain peace and stability; wind and rain will fall in their proper seasons, and the crops will ripen. The sentient beings within the country will be free from illness and live in peace and happiness; furthermore, there will be no harassment or disturbance by violent yakṣas and other spirits, and all evil omens will completely vanish.
Furthermore, Kṣatriya consecrated kings and others shall all obtain an increase in lifespan and physical strength, remaining free from illness and possessing mastery. "Venerable Ānanda!

If emperors, queens, consorts, crown princes, sons of kings, high ministers, counselors, palace ladies, officials, or the common people suffer from illness or other calamities and misfortunes, they should likewise reverently fashion images of the seven Buddhas, recite this sutra, light lamps, create banners, release living beings, and make offerings with utmost sincerity by burning incense and scattering flowers; thus, their suffering from illness will be eliminated, and they shall be liberated from all hardships.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Bodhisattva Rescuer from Peril:
"Virtuous man! How can a life that has already been exhausted be increased?"
The Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta said:
"Virtuous One! Have you not heard the Tathāgata speak of the nine types of untimely death?"

Therefore, the World-Honored One taught him spells and medicines to provide relief according to his condition; he was instructed to light lamps, create banners, and cultivate various meritorious deeds, for by cultivating merit, one may prolong one's lifespan.
Ānanda asked, "What are the nine untimely deaths?
The Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla replied:

"First, there are sentient beings who fall ill; though their condition is slight, they lack medicine and a caregiver. Even if they encounter a physician, the physician does not administer medicine. Though they ought not to die, they meet with an untimely death.

Furthermore, they place their faith in worldly demons, heretics, and sorcerers who falsely proclaim calamities and blessings. Consequently, they become terrified and agitated, losing their mental composure. They consult diviners for good or bad fortune, slaughter living beings, offer sacrifices to spirits, summon malevolent ghosts, and pray for blessings and grace, hoping to prolong their lives—yet in the end, they cannot achieve this. Through such foolish delusion and inverted views, they cause themselves to meet an untimely death and enter hell from which there is no time of escape."
Second, they are unexpectedly executed by the laws of the king.
Third, through hunting, sporting, indulgence in lust, and addiction to wine, they become dissolute and immoderate, whereby non-human spirits unexpectedly seize their vital essence.
Fourth, they are suddenly burned by fire.
Fifth, they are suddenly drowned by water.
Sixth, they are suddenly devoured by various kinds of evil beasts.
Seventh, they fall precipitously from mountain cliffs.
Eighth, they are suddenly struck and harmed by poisons, malevolent incantations, curses, or the ghosts of the risen dead.
Ninth, being afflicted by hunger and thirst, one dies a sudden death because one cannot obtain food or drink.
These, O Tathāgata, are the nine kinds of sudden death briefly explained; furthermore, there are immeasurable other forms of sudden death that are difficult to describe in full.
"Furthermore, Ānanda! That King Yama maintains the registers of all those in the world.

If there are sentient beings who are unfilial, commit the five heinous crimes, insult or disparage the Triple Gem, subvert the laws between sovereign and subject, or violate their prohibitive precepts, King Yama, the Lord of Dharma, shall examine and punish them according to the gravity of their offenses."

Therefore, I now exhort all sentient beings to light lamps, create banners, release living beings, and cultivate merit, so that they may cross over suffering and calamity and not encounter various hardships.
At that time, there were twelve yakṣa generals in the assembly, all seated together in the gathering.
Their names were: the General Piṅgala, and the General Vajra.
The Great General Mikhila, the Great General Anila, the Great General Manila, the Great General Sanila,
the Great General Indara, and the Great General Paila.
The Great General Bahuhura, the Great General Cendala, the Great General Cūdala,
and the Great General Vikala— these twelve yakṣa generals,
each with a retinue of seven thousand yakṣas, simultaneously raised their voices and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By virtue of the Buddha’s majestic power, we have now been able to hear the names of the seven Tathāgatas; thus, we shall no longer have any fear regarding the various evil realms.”

We shall lead one another, with a single mind, until the end of our lives, taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; we vow to bear the burden of all sentient beings, acting for their benefit, welfare, and peace and happiness.

In whatever city, village, or secluded forest this sutra may circulate and be recited, or wherever one upholds the names of the seven Buddhas and reverently makes offerings to them, we and our retinues shall protect that person, causing them to escape all calamities and ensuring that all their aspirations and requests are fully satisfied.

If there are those who suffer from illness or calamity and seek deliverance, they should likewise recite this sutra; using threads of five colors, they should tie my name into knots, and once their wishes are fulfilled, they should then untie the knots.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the yakṣa generals, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"O Great Yakṣa Generals!
If you wish to repay the kindness and virtue of the seven Tathāgatas of the past Buddhas, you should always benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings in this manner."
At that time, there were many members of the celestial assembly in the gathering whose wisdom was meager, and they thought to themselves:
"How is it that those who merely hear the names of the Tathāgatas currently residing in Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River obtain such boundless and supreme merit?"
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of devas, immediately entered the profound and wondrous samādhi called "Invoking All Tathāgatas."
As soon as they had entered meditative absorption, the entire trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and celestial flowers and celestial powdered incense rained down.
Having witnessed these signs, those seven Tathāgatas each came from their respective lands to the Sahā world to exchange greetings with Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

At that time, by the power of his original vows from previous lives, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, sat down in his respective place upon each lion throne adorned with celestial jewels. Surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas, the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others—both human and non-human—as well as kings, princes, members of the inner court and their consorts, along with various ministers, brahmins, elders, and householders, he preached the Dharma for them.
At that time, when the assembly of devas saw that the Tathāgata had already gathered like clouds, they were filled with great wonder, and their doubts were dispelled.
Then the great multitude, marveling at what had never occurred before, praised him with one voice, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent, Śākyamuni Tathāgata!
You have benefited us by dispelling our doubts and causing those Tathāgatas to all arrive here.

Then, the great assembly, each according to their own power, made offerings to the Tathāgata with exquisite incense, flowers, various necklaces, and celestial music; they circumambulated him seven times to the right, joined their palms in reverent salutation, and praised him, saying:
"How rare! How extraordinary!"
How marvelous!
The profound realm of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is inconceivable; through the power of their prior vows and skillful means, they together manifest such extraordinary signs.
At that time, the great assembly each made a vow, wishing that all sentient beings might attain such a supreme samādhi of the Tathāgata.
Then Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, circumambulated the Buddha seven times, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent! Excellent!
The Tathāgata’s power of meditative concentration is inconceivable; through the power of his original vows and his skillful means, he brings sentient beings to maturity.

I only pray that you will expound for us a mantra of great power, which can serve as a refuge for sentient beings of meager merit in future ages who are beset by illness and affliction, by all calamities involving the sun, moon, and stars, by epidemics and malevolent spirits, and by those traveling on perilous paths who encounter various terrors, thereby enabling them to attain peace and security.

If those sentient beings, regarding this divine mantra, either write it themselves, teach others to write it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, or extensively explain it to others, they will constantly be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas. The Buddhas will personally manifest their bodies to cause their aspirations to be fulfilled; they shall not fall into the evil realms, nor shall they suffer untimely death.
At that time, all the Tathāgatas praised Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

"This is through our majestic spiritual power that we have caused you to make this request; out of compassion for sentient beings, so that they may be freed from all suffering and hardship, we shall speak this divine mantra.
You should listen attentively and reflect upon it well; we shall now explain it for you."

Mañjuśrī! There is a great divine mantra called "The Tathāgata’s Power of Concentration and Lapis Lazuli Light. If any man or woman writes it down, recites it, reverently makes offerings to it, and gives rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings, all their aspirations and requests shall be fulfilled; the Buddhas will manifest before them to protect and mind them, they shall be freed from all obstacles and afflictions, and they shall be born in a Buddha-land.
Then the seven Tathāgatas, with a single voice, spoke this mantra:
"Tadyathā | gumye gumye | gumnime | nime | hīḥ."
maitri maitri svāhā tathāgatasamādhy-adhiṣṭhite adhimaitri pāle.
Pāpa-śodhani sarva-pāpāni śamayantu bhūtaḥ.
Candā-mi-vo-mi-ku-mi-buddha-dharaṇi-pāriśuddhi-tan-mi-ni-tan-mi.
mīlu mīlu mīlu śike liye sarva karomi ṭindyuḥ.
Nimbāṇi-buddhe subuddhe buddhoddite ṣaṇṇavakṣa-dume.
Sarvatathāgata-samaye samayas tvam anupraviṣṭo 'si | Sarvabuddhabodhisattvasamayas tvam samayaḥ samayaḥ ||
Prakṣveḍamānāḥ sarva-īty-upadravāḥ sarva-vighnāś ca.
Sarvasattvānāṃ buraṇe buraṇe buraṇaye sarvāśāṃ pūraya.
*Paritāpe sarvabhayebhyaḥ kṣemebhyaḥ svāhā.* At that time,
when the seven Buddhas spoke this mantra, light shone everywhere, the great earth shook, and various miraculous transformations manifested all at once.

At that time, having witnessed this event, the great assembly each offered celestial fragrant flowers, ointments, and powdered incense to the Buddha according to their respective means; they all cried out, "Excellent! and circumambulated him seven times to the right.
Those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, raised their voices in unison and declared:
"All you great assemblies of devas and humans, you should know this:

if there are good men or good women—whether kings, princes, queens, ministers, or commoners—who receive, uphold, read, recite, hear, or explain this dhāraṇī; who offer exquisite incense and flowers to the scripture; who put on new, clean garments and dwell in a pure place; who observe the eightfold precepts and always give rise to compassion for all sentient beings; by making such offerings, they shall obtain immeasurable merit."
Furthermore, if there is anyone who has a prayer or aspiration, they should fashion images of these seven Buddhas.
In a quiet place, they should make offerings with various incenses and flowers, hanging silken banners and canopies, providing exquisite food and drink, as well as various musical performances;
and they should also make offerings to the Bodhisattvas and devas who are present before the Buddhas.

Sitting upright as before while reciting the mantra, if one observes the eightfold fast for seven days and completes one thousand and eight recitations, all those Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas will protect and keep them in mind;
the Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, along with Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings, will also come to guard and defend this person. All [five...]
The five crimes of immediate retribution and all karmic obstructions will be entirely extinguished;
one shall be free from illness and enjoy longevity, and shall suffer neither untimely death nor various epidemics.
Should thieves and bandits from other regions seek to invade the borders, or should there be strife, war, litigation, enmity, famine, drought, or floods—such fears as these shall all be eliminated.
“Together we shall give rise to a heart of loving-kindness, like that of parents; whatever they may wish or seek, there shall be nothing that does not fulfill their intent.
